analysis.one_liner: Exempts tribal businesses on tribal land from federal law protecting workers' right to unionize.
analysis.headline: A Senate committee favorably reported the bill in February 2017 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never got a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to exclude Native American tribes, and any business or institution a tribe owns and operates on its own land, from the federal law that guarantees most private-sector workers the right to form unions, bargain collectively, and be free from unfair labor practices. In practice, this would cover tribal casinos, hotels, and other commercial operations that are among the largest private employers on tribal land. Supporters framed it as a matter of tribal sovereignty, putting tribes on the same footing as states and local governments, which are also outside the NLRA. The bill cleared committee but never received a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments that own and operate casinos, hotels, and other enterprises on their land would gain freedom from National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction, including union organizing drives and unfair-labor-practice cases brought by their employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal governments running casinos and enterprises

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds tribes, and any enterprise or institution owned and operated by a tribe and located on its Indian lands, to the definition of excluded employers under the National Labor Relations Act.
Excluded employers are not subject to NLRA requirements to allow union formation, collective bargaining, and collective action, and not barred from unfair labor practices.
Supporters describe this as clarifying tribal sovereignty over labor matters on Indian lands, consistent with the treatment of state and local governments, which the NLRA also does not cover.

analysis.who_pays: Employees at tribal casinos and other tribal enterprises on tribal land would lose the federal right to organize, bargain collectively, and file unfair-labor-practice charges with the National Labor Relations Board.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers at tribal businesses on tribal land

drawbacks.text: Employees at tribal enterprises on tribal land would lose NLRA protections against unfair labor practices and their federal right to unionize and bargain collectively, and tribal commercial operations, including casinos, are large private employers whose workers would have no federal labor-law floor.

The bill's exemption covered not only tribal governmental functions but any enterprise owned and operated by a tribe on its land, so major commercial operations would be treated like governments rather than ordinary employers.

Supporters' counterargument: tribes are sovereign governments, states and local governments are already exempt from the NLRA, and federal labor law over tribal employers was extended by the National Labor Relations Board rather than by Congress, so the bill restores the balance tribes say Congress intended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine sovereignty argument: the NLRA never mentioned tribes, states and local governments are already exempt, and a board decision rather than an act of Congress extended federal jurisdiction over tribal employers. But the exemption as written would apply to all commercial enterprises on tribal land, including large casinos and resorts, and would fall on the employees of those businesses, who are often tribal members themselves and would lose the only federal labor-law protections they have. The bill offered no substitute worker protections, so the practical trade is clear sovereignty for tribal governments in exchange for a real loss of rights for their employees.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Indian Affairs Committee reported the bill favorably in February 2017 and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but no senator ever brought it up for a vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 9, 2017 and referred to the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs.
On February 8, 2017 the committee ordered the bill reported favorably, and on February 17 it was reported without amendment, with written report 115-3.
On February 17, 2017 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 9, meaning it was ready to be called up, but it never came to a floor vote.
No further action occurred for the rest of the 115th Congress, which ended January 3, 2019, so the bill never became law.
The bill would have amended the National Labor Relations Act to exclude tribes and tribal enterprises and institutions on tribal land from NLRA employer requirements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employees at tribal casinos and enterprises kept their federal rights to unionize and file unfair-labor-practice charges, and unions retained jurisdiction there, because the bill died without a vote. Tribal governments seeking the exemption gained nothing, and the NLRB's existing jurisdiction over tribal enterprises on tribal land stands.

for.name: Jerry Moran
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 9, 2017, joined by 13 Republican colleagues.

for.name: Senate Committee on Indian Affairs
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction, Republican-led in the 115th Congress
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably on February 8, 2017 and reported it without amendment on February 17, 2017 (Report 115-3), placing it on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader's office, controls the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up for a vote; it sat on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders for the remainder of the 115th Congress with no floor action.

against.name: AFL-CIO and labor unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would strip federal labor protections from workers at tribal casinos and other tribal enterprises.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 original sponsors were Republicans and no Democrats cosponsored; the Republican-led committee reported it favorably, but the bill never reached the floor, so no recorded vote exists to measure the full chamber's split.

industries.industry: Tribal casinos and tribal enterprises on tribal land
industries.note: The bill would have exempted any enterprise owned and operated by a tribe on its land from the NLRA, freeing tribal casinos, hotels, and other commercial operations from union drives and NLRB cases. The gain came at the direct cost of their employees' federal labor rights, and those employees are often tribal members themselves.

Unions would lose jurisdiction over workplaces on tribal land, closing off thousands of potential members at tribal casinos and resorts. Their interest in the bill ran alongside the workers they would have represented.
